planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; evergreen climbing hydrangea is less cold-hardy than the deciduous climbing hydrangea and benefits from a sheltered site.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; evergreen climbing hydrangea is less cold-hardy than the deciduous climbing hydrangea and benefits from a sheltered site. Glossy, leathery, evergreen leaves cover a self-clinging vine that attaches to walls, trellises, and tree trunks by aerial roots much like its more familiar deciduous relative, producing flat, lacecap clusters of small fertile flowers surrounded by larger, showy white sterile florets in summer. Native to cloud forests of Mexico and Central America, it holds its foliage year-round in mild climates, providing continuous coverage on a north-facing wall or shaded fence unlike the winter-bare deciduous climbing hydrangea. Provide a sturdy support for the self-clinging stems, keep soil consistently moist, and mulch well to protect roots in the colder parts of its hardiness range.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a sturdy trellis or arbor; variegated chocolate vine is a vigorous twining climber and needs a strong support, plus occasional pruning to control spread.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near a sturdy trellis or arbor; variegated chocolate vine is a vigorous twining climber and needs a strong support, plus occasional pruning to control spread. Palmate, five-lobed leaves are irregularly splashed and marbled in creamy white, a bright variegated counterpart to the plain green species, twining vigorously up any nearby support and producing small, chocolate-scented, maroon-purple flowers in spring, occasionally followed by unusual sausage-shaped purple fruit with sweet, edible pulp in favorable conditions. Its vigorous, twining growth can become aggressive and self-seed in mild climates, so site it where its spread can be managed and monitor for volunteer seedlings, particularly since escaped chocolate vine has become invasive in parts of the eastern United States. Prune hard in late winter to control size and shape, and provide a sturdy arbor, fence, or trellis strong enough to support its vigorous twining growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; this selection has smaller, finer leaves than typical Virginia creeper and clings tightly to masonry and wood.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; this selection has smaller, finer leaves than typical Virginia creeper and clings tightly to masonry and wood. A finer-textured, smaller-leaved selection of the native Virginia creeper, it clings tightly to brick, stone, and wood surfaces with adhesive tendril discs, covering walls and structures densely with palmate, five-lobed leaves that turn a brilliant scarlet-red in fall, one of the showiest native fall foliage displays of any vine. Extremely tough and adaptable, tolerating poor soil, drought, shade, and urban pollution, it provides valuable dark blue berries for birds in fall and is a larval host plant for several native moth species. Prune as needed to keep growth away from windows, gutters, and shingles, since the adhesive tendrils can damage some building surfaces and are difficult to remove once attached.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; Boston ivy clings tightly to masonry surfaces and is difficult to remove once established, so site carefully.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging tendrils; Boston ivy clings tightly to masonry surfaces and is difficult to remove once established, so site carefully. One of the original introduced forms of the classic ivy-league-covering vine, it produces smaller, more deeply three-lobed leaves emerging purplish-bronze in spring before maturing to glossy green and turning a spectacular scarlet-crimson in fall, clinging tightly to brick and stone with adhesive tendril discs to blanket entire building facades. Extremely vigorous and self-clinging, it needs no additional support once established but can grow large enough to obscure windows and gutters if not pruned, and removing an established planting from masonry can leave persistent tendril residue. Prune annually to keep growth away from windows, doors, and roof edges, and consider the vine's vigorous, decades-long coverage potential before planting against a valued building surface.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Plants Database

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; this slow-establishing evergreen vine rewards patience with years of low-maintenance coverage once mature.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade near a wall or sturdy support for the self-clinging aerial roots; this slow-establishing evergreen vine rewards patience with years of low-maintenance coverage once mature. Glossy, leathery, evergreen leaves cling self-sufficiently to a wall, tree trunk, or fence by aerial roots much like climbing hydrangea, producing frothy, creamy-white clusters of small flowers in late summer when few other climbing shrubs are blooming. Native to forests of China, it is slower to establish than more vigorous climbing vines, often taking several years before it begins climbing in earnest, but once established requires little maintenance and holds its evergreen foliage through mild winters better than deciduous climbing hydrangea relatives. Provide consistent moisture during establishment, be patient during the slow early years of growth, and site on a shaded wall or trunk where its self-clinging roots can attach.

planting.note: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a trellis or fence for the twining stems; variegated confederate jasmine holds its cream-margined variegation best in bright light.

directions: Plant container-grown vines in spring in average, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade near a trellis or fence for the twining stems; variegated confederate jasmine holds its cream-margined variegation best in bright light. Glossy, dark green leaves are irregularly edged in creamy white, often blushed pink on new growth in cooler weather, providing year-round variegated color even outside the plant's intensely fragrant late-spring flowering period, when small, pinwheel-shaped white flowers cover the twining vine with classic jasmine scent. Slightly less vigorous and cold-hardy than the plain green species, it still makes a fine trellis, fence, or mailbox-post vine in warm-climate gardens or a colorful container specimen further north, brought indoors or into a greenhouse for winter outside its hardiness range. Provide a support for the twining stems, water regularly during establishment, and prune after flowering to control size and shape.
